title: “IF IT’S GOD’S WILL, EVERYTHING WILL FALL INTO PLACE” — THE COMFORTING LIE THAT MAY BE KEEPING YOU FROM YOUR CALLING
paragraphs: “IF IT’S GOD’S WILL, EVERYTHING WILL FALL INTO PLACE” — THE COMFORTING LIE THAT MAY BE KEEPING YOU FROM YOUR CALLING
What if the resistance you are desperately praying God would remove is not evidence that you are outside His will, but part of the very journey through which He is transforming you?
You prayed.
You waited.
You surrendered what you thought you wanted. You asked God for direction. You cried behind closed doors, opened your Bible, and begged Him to make everything clear.
And somehow, everything became more complicated.

The opportunity disappeared. The relationship fell apart. The finances became tighter. The people you thought would support you walked away. The door you were convinced God had opened suddenly slammed shut.
Then someone looked at you and said something that sounded incredibly spiritual:
“If it’s really God’s will, everything will fall into place.”
So you started questioning everything.
Maybe you heard God wrong.
Maybe you lacked faith.
Maybe you weren't praying enough.
Maybe God was disappointed in you.
Maybe the struggle itself was His way of telling you to stop.
But before you abandon something simply because it has become difficult, there is a question you desperately need to confront.
Who told you that the will of God would always be comfortable?
Because it wasn't Jesus.
It wasn't the apostles.
And it certainly wasn't the testimony of Scripture.

Somewhere along the way, modern Christianity began confusing divine direction with personal convenience. We started interpreting comfort as confirmation, inconvenience as rejection, financial prosperity as approval, and suffering as evidence that something must have gone spiritually wrong.
We developed a version of Christianity where God supposedly proves His presence by removing everything that makes us uncomfortable.
But that theology collapses at the foot of the cross.
If an easy path were the ultimate evidence of God's will, then what would we make of Jesus Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane?
Imagine that night.
The darkness. The loneliness. The disciples struggling to stay awake. The weight of what was coming.
Jesus knew betrayal was approaching. He knew the humiliation, rejection, suffering, and crucifixion that awaited Him.
And He prayed:
“Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
The original Greek contains these deeply significant words:
πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω.
Plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō.
“Nevertheless, not my will, but Yours be done.”
The Greek word θέλημα (thelēma) refers to will, desire, or intention. The word γινέσθω (ginesthō) carries the sense of something coming to pass or taking place.
Jesus was not asking the Father to prove His will by making the journey painless.
He was submitting to the Father's will despite knowing how painful the journey would be.
Let that sink in.
The most perfectly obedient person who ever walked this earth experienced unimaginable suffering while fulfilling the Father's redemptive purpose.
Jesus was not outside God's will because He was suffering.
His sacrificial death was central to God's plan of salvation.
Acts 2:23 declares that Jesus was delivered according to the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, while also holding those responsible for His crucifixion accountable.
The cross was not a divine accident.
What appeared to be a catastrophic defeat became the very means through which sinners could receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life through Christ.
And three days later, the resurrection revealed that death did not have the final word.
If you had judged God's faithfulness by what you saw on Friday, you would have misunderstood what God accomplished on Sunday.
Perhaps that is where some of us are living right now.
Somewhere between the pain of Friday and the hope of Sunday.

You cannot see how the pieces fit together. You cannot understand why certain prayers remain unanswered. You are exhausted from trying to make sense of a season that feels nothing like the life you imagined.

And although Scripture does not promise that every earthly disappointment will be reversed, it does assure believers that suffering cannot separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:35–39).
Your circumstances are not the ultimate measure of His faithfulness.
Consider the apostle Paul.
In 1 Corinthians 16:9, he wrote:
“For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.”
Read that again.
An open door.
And many adversaries.
Not an open door without opposition.
Not an open door surrounded by applause.
Not an open door where everything became financially, emotionally, and physically convenient.
The original Greek reads:
θύρα γάρ μοι ἀνέῳγεν μεγάλη καὶ ἐνεργής, καὶ ἀντικείμενοι πολλοί.
The sense is that a great and effective door had opened for Paul, and there were many who opposed him.
The opportunity and the opposition existed simultaneously.
Paul did not automatically interpret resistance as evidence that God had closed the door.
He recognized that meaningful Gospel ministry could exist in the middle of intense opposition.
Yet Scripture also records occasions when God genuinely redirected Paul.
In Acts 16:6–10, the Holy Spirit prevented Paul and his companions from preaching in certain regions before directing them toward Macedonia.
This gives us an essential biblical balance.
Not every obstacle means you should stop.
But not every obstacle means you should keep going, either.

Sometimes God redirects us. Sometimes obedience requires perseverance. Sometimes our difficulties are consequences of our own foolish decisions. Sometimes we suffer because we live in a fallen world. Sometimes we suffer precisely because we are following Christ.
Spiritual discernment requires more than interpreting circumstances according to what we desperately want to believe.
It requires Scripture, prayer, wisdom, humility, godly counsel, and a willingness to surrender even our most cherished plans.
Because there is another uncomfortable truth we rarely discuss.
Just because everything is falling into place does not mean God approves of where you are going.
Remember Jonah?
God instructed him to go to Nineveh.
Jonah decided to go in the opposite direction.
And what happened?
He found a ship.
There was transportation available. He had enough money to pay the fare. Everything seemed to align conveniently for his escape.
Jonah 1:3 records that he went down to Joppa, found a ship going to Tarshish, paid the fare, and boarded it.
Imagine interpreting that through today's popular Christian sayings.
“The door opened!”
“The resources were provided!”
“Everything aligned perfectly!”
“It must be God's will!”
Except it wasn't.
Jonah was deliberately running from what God had commanded.
The convenient opportunity was not divine approval.
And the storm that followed was not evidence that God had abandoned him.
In Jonah's particular story, God used the storm to interrupt his disobedience and eventually bring him back toward his commission.
Sometimes the thing you call a blessing is enabling your rebellion.
Sometimes the thing you call an inconvenience is exposing your pride.
Sometimes the door you desperately want opened leads somewhere Scripture has already warned you not to go.
An available opportunity is not automatically a divine assignment.
A peaceful feeling is not automatically the voice of the Holy Spirit.
A profitable decision is not automatically a righteous decision.
And a difficult season is not automatically evidence of God's absence.
This is why we must stop allowing our emotions and circumstances to become the final authority over our theology.
God has already given us something more trustworthy.
His Word.
Psalm 119:105 declares:
“Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.”
The original Hebrew reads:
נֵר־לְרַגְלִי דְבָרֶךָ וְאוֹר לִנְתִיבָתִי
Ner leragli devarekha, ve'or lintivati.
“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.”
The Hebrew word נֵר (ner) means a lamp, while אוֹר (or) means light.
Notice the imagery.
A lamp illuminating your feet and your path.
Not a guarantee that you will see every detail of your future.
Not a promise that the road will be free of danger.
Not an assurance that you will understand every painful chapter before taking another step.
God's Word gives direction for faithful living even when the future remains uncertain.
And sometimes the hardest part of faith is obeying what God has clearly revealed while surrendering what He has not.
You want the entire map.
You want guarantees.

You want to know whether the business will succeed, whether the relationship will survive, whether the ministry will grow, whether your family will understand, and whether everything you sacrificed will eventually make sense.
But biblical faith is not certainty that your preferred outcome will happen.
It is confidence in the character of God, even when the outcome remains unknown.
Look at Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego standing before Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 3.
They believed God was able to deliver them from the fiery furnace.
But their obedience did not depend upon being rescued.
“But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods.” — Daniel 3:18, KJV
That is a level of faith many of us struggle to understand.
God can deliver us.
But even if He does not deliver us in the way we desire, we will not bow.
Even if the promotion never comes.
Even if the diagnosis does not change.
Even if the person never apologizes.
Even if the ministry never becomes famous.
Even if obedience costs us something we desperately wanted to keep.
Christ is still worthy.
That is faith that has moved beyond treating God as a means of obtaining a comfortable life.
That is faith rooted in who God is.
And perhaps this is where the Holy Spirit is confronting something deeper within us.
Have we been seeking God's will, or have we been seeking God's approval for our own will?
Have we been asking Him to lead us, or asking Him to guarantee the future we already designed?
Would we still follow Jesus if following Him cost us the very thing we were hoping He would give us?
These are not easy questions.
They expose the hidden negotiations we sometimes disguise as prayer.
“Lord, I will trust You, as long as You restore this relationship.”
“Lord, I will serve You, as long as You bless my plans.”
“Lord, I will obey You, as long as obedience doesn't cost me too much.”
But Jesus never invited us into a relationship built upon those conditions.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
The Greek word translated as “deny” is ἀρνησάσθω (arnēsasthō), meaning to deny or disown oneself.
In this context, Jesus is calling His followers to relinquish self-rule and submit to Him.
The Christian life is not about making Jesus a supporting character in the story of our ambitions.
It is about recognizing Him as Lord.
And surrendering to His lordship does not mean tolerating abuse, remaining in dangerous situations, ignoring medical needs, or recklessly pursuing something simply because it is difficult.
Seeking safety, receiving help, establishing appropriate boundaries, and accepting wise counsel can all be consistent with faithful Christian living.
Suffering itself is not proof of righteousness.
First Peter 4:15–16 distinguishes suffering for wrongdoing from suffering as a Christian.
The question is not merely whether something is painful.
The question is whether our response is faithful to Christ.
Maybe you need to persevere.
Maybe you need to repent.
Maybe you need to walk away.
Maybe you need to apologize.
Maybe you need to stop calling your stubbornness faith.
Maybe you need to stop calling your fear discernment.
And maybe you need to stop demanding that God explain Himself before you are willing to obey what He has already made clear.
Romans 12:2 teaches that discerning God's will is connected to the transformation and renewal of our minds.
The Greek word δοκιμάζειν (dokimazein) means to examine, test, discern, or approve.
Biblical discernment is not simply searching for convenient coincidences.
It involves a mind increasingly transformed by God's truth.

Ask whether your decision contradicts Scripture. Examine your motives. Seek mature biblical counsel. Pray for wisdom. Consider your responsibilities. Remain willing to be corrected. Hold your personal plans with open hands.
And remember that God's revealed will includes your sanctification (1 Thessalonians 4:3), gratitude in Christ (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and a life that honors Him.
You may not receive an immediate answer concerning every personal decision.
But you can begin obeying what He has already revealed.
Perhaps you have spent years carrying shame because your life did not unfold the way you expected.
You thought you would be further ahead.
You thought your marriage would look different.
You thought your children would make different choices.
You thought your prayers would have been answered by now.
You thought that following Jesus meant you would never find yourself crying over circumstances you could not control.
And somewhere in the disappointment, you began wondering whether God still loved you.
Please remember what the Gospel actually declares.
Your salvation is not secured by how smoothly your life unfolds.
It is not earned by your accomplishments.
It is not measured by your financial success.
It is not dependent upon your ability to understand everything God permits.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe.
The scandal of our sin meets the immeasurable grace of a Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
That is why your failures do not have to become your final identity.
Your past does not have to remain your master.
Your shame does not have to dictate your future.
In Christ, forgiveness is real. Reconciliation with God is possible. Transformation begins through His grace.
This does not mean every earthly loss will be restored exactly as you imagined.
It means that those who belong to Christ possess a hope greater than anything this fallen world can take away.
Romans 8:28 is often quoted as a promise that everything will eventually work out according to our preferences.
But the following verse reveals the deeper purpose.
Romans 8:29 speaks of believers being conformed to the image of God's Son.
The good God is working toward is not merely our convenience.
It is ultimately connected to His redemptive purpose and our conformity to Christ.
God's purpose is greater than making your circumstances comfortable. He is transforming you into the likeness of His Son.
And that transformation may challenge the very things you once believed you could never live without.
So, is the statement “If it's God's will, everything will fall into place” actually biblical?
Only if we understand it to mean that God's sovereign purposes will ultimately stand.
Isaiah 46:10 affirms that God's counsel will stand and that He will accomplish His purpose.
But Scripture never promises that obedience will make every circumstance convenient, that faithful Christians will avoid suffering, or that every personal dream will eventually become reality.
God's will is not always the easiest road.
Jesus Himself warned His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33, KJV
Our confidence is not that we will never encounter trouble.
Our confidence is that Christ has overcome.
There is an enormous difference.
If this article has exposed something you have been quietly wrestling with, take a moment to be spiritually honest.
Something that takes only a few seconds of your time could place biblical encouragement in front of someone who has been silently losing hope.
We want to continue building a community where people are not merely entertained by Christianity but challenged to know Jesus, understand His Word, repent of sin, and grow in genuine faith.
Ministry requires time, resources, dedication, and the faithful generosity of people who believe that biblical truth is worth sharing.

Galatians 6:6 teaches the importance of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come willingly from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.

It is not a payment for God's favor, a requirement for salvation, or an obligation that replaces your responsibilities to your family or local church. Rather, it is an opportunity to participate in a ministry whose mission you believe is worth supporting.
Because this was never supposed to be about building our own kingdom.
It is about faithfully serving the King.
Tonight, when you are alone with the questions nobody else hears, remember Gethsemane.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the Savior who calls you to trust Him is not unfamiliar with suffering.
You do not need to pretend that the pain is beautiful.
You do not need to manufacture an explanation for everything that has happened.
You do not need to know how every piece of your life will fit together before you can faithfully follow Jesus.
You can grieve and still believe.
You can tremble and still obey.
You can have unanswered questions and still cling to Christ.
And when you stumble, you can return to Him in repentance, trusting in His mercy rather than hiding behind your shame.
Perhaps the prayer you need today is no longer, “Lord, make everything fall into place.”
Perhaps it is:

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for confusing my desires with Your will. Renew my mind through Your Word. Give me wisdom to recognize Your direction, humility to accept Your correction, courage to obey You, and faith to trust You when I cannot understand. Let my life glorify You, even when the road is difficult. Not my will, but Yours be done. Amen.”
The world may tell you that everything must fall into place before you can have peace.
The Gospel points you toward a Savior who offers peace even in the midst of tribulation.
And if you ever find yourself wondering whether a painful road can still lead somewhere meaningful, remember what stood between Gethsemane and the resurrection.
A cross.
Never mistake the difficulty of the road for the absence of the Savior. The hands that were pierced for your redemption are worthy of your trust, even when you cannot see what lies ahead.
